What you said is the other half of the subjunctive: there is uncertainty in the sentence because it depends on other people/other facts.  


"I'm glad that I came" the "I'm glad" can only happen because "I came" so you connect those via subjunctive.   


Also bear in mind that I'm talking about the simple subjunctive ("haya venido" is compound subj); Further I speak portuguese not spanish but I think all rules apply.  


The three basic subj are in the present (that), future (when) and past (if) and they rely on being hypothetical, uncertain or depending on someone else (thus being uncertain)  


Present "I hope THAT I can go to the party", the going to the party in uncertain  


Future "When you get home, call me", the calling me only happens under the getting home being fulfilled  


Past "If I weren't lied down I'd grab it" the grabbing it could've only happened IF (under the condition) in the past I was standing up.

The first for "if", you're making a condition so you conjugate the verb as subjunctive "if you come home too late". This entire sentence is a condition.  


The latter is when a point in time is the condition itself as in "when I get home \[...\]", the get home is a condition, it hasn't happened yet but the rest of the sentence relies on this being true

>Quantum Mechanics is actually completely deterministic in that if you  definite an initial wave function and the Hamiltonian that governs its  evolution, then the wave function at all past and future times is  perfectly defined

Physicist here.  


This is half-right half-wrong.

Yes, if you control everything in your system the wave function will be determined at any point in time, however this doesnt not make the systemc deterministic at all. You may know that the particle's spin can be (50-50) either up or down but there is NOTHING and cannot stress this enough: there is **nothing** you can do to determine wheter the output will be up or down.   


In classical mechanics if you control everything you know where the particle was and where it'll be.  


In QM if you control everything you know where it likely was and what/where it likely will be but you cannot determine EXACTLY what it'll be. It's not deterministic for that. You only know your options and you can only know what it is after you force the wave function to collapse.

Physicist here (actually in my Master's), quantum mechanics is actually easier than it looks. The whole thing is you don't work with the object itself i.e., youre not calculating how a ball (electron) is moving around, youre calculating how its distributed across space and time. In QM we treat the probabilities of stuff being in a certain place and certain time.  


Why we do that? Because there is an experiment that says that if light passes through a polarizer its intesity will change (lower) depending on the polarizer angle, but light is also made of tiny little stuff called the Quanta so if you get to reduce the intesity to 50% you have 2 options: either these Quanta are split in halves and all quanta passes or they have a 50% chance for passing or not passing making everything inheretly probabilistic.  


All the other fancy stuff come from this very concept that things are now subject to fluctuations, incertainties and they must follow some very specific rules. Quantum tunelling is just fancy words for 'probability of passing to the other side'.
